drapeaux.note: Lords quotations (“between 5 and 6 million”, “some 5 million”, “the inspectorates should be merged together”) taken from Hansard, HL Deb 30 January 1973, as retrieved through a page summarizer; the Asquith paraphrase and the statutory phrase “so far as is reasonably practicable” are not quotations from a page read in full.

titre: In 1974, a British Law Sets a General Duty of Safety
accroche: In the early 1970s, millions of British employees were covered by no safety law. In 1974, a law sets a principle.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1970, in the United Kingdom, workplace safety law is scattered across statutes passed decades apart for each sector (mines, factories, offices and shops), each with its own technical rules. An inquiry committee chaired by Lord Robens (Alfred Robens) is tasked with examining this state of the law. Before the House of Lords, in January 1973, two peers put numbers on the finding: Lord Avebury speaks of “between 5 and 6 million” workers who are not covered by any legislation, Lord Drumalbyn of “some 5 million” who fall outside the scope of existing provisions.

## A Principle Rather Than One More Law

The Robens report, published in 1972, does not recommend adding one more law to this pile. Before the House of Lords, Lord Drumalbyn sums up its proposals: bring the main laws together under a single framework act that sets out the basic responsibilities of employers and employees, and create a new institution to administer it. Lord Avebury calls in that same debate for “the inspectorates” to “be merged together.” The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act receives royal assent on July 31, 1974, and comes into force on the following October 1. It creates the Health and Safety Commission and the Health and Safety Executive, which will absorb the factory inspectorate and the mines inspectorate; by its section 3, it also extends a duty of safety toward persons who are not its employees, and toward self-employed workers in certain designated activities such as construction, asbestos, or gas.

## A Formula Older Than the Law

The law's central duty, to ensure safety “so far as is reasonably practicable,” was not invented for the occasion. The formula already appeared in the Coal Mines Act of 1911, and had been examined by the courts in *Coltness Iron Co v. Sharp* (1938). It was the English Court of Appeal's decision in *Edwards v. National Coal Board* (1949), handed down after the death of a miner in a roof fall, that fixed its interpretation: Judge Asquith defines the expression there as a weighing of the size of the risk, on one side, against the cost and difficulty of removing it, on the other; the employer is excused from acting only if that cost is grossly disproportionate to the risk, the risk then being negligible in light of the sacrifice demanded. In 1974, Parliament extends to the entire British economy a formula already written into the mines law in 1911, whose meaning the courts had clarified in 1938, then in 1949.

repere.texte: Section 2 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act requires the employer to ensure, “so far as is reasonably practicable,” the health, safety, and welfare at work of their employees.
repere.source: United Kingdom, legislation.gov.uk, Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, section 2

carte.punch: Faced with safety laws scattered by sector, a British law sets a general duty.
carte.idee: In the Lords in 1973, speakers mention 5 to 6 million British workers covered by no safety law. The 1974 Health and Safety at Work Act sets a general duty applying to every employer: a formula that had already existed in English law since 1911.
carte.source_courte: Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, c. 37

quiz.question: What does the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act of 1974 change in the way workplace safety is legislated in the United Kingdom?
choix: It adds further technical rules to the sector-specific laws already in force
It transfers all labor regulation to a European authority
It removes every legal obligation and lets employers organize freely among themselves
It sets a general duty of safety, the same for every employer, rather than adding sector-specific technical rules
quiz.explication: Following the Robens report, as Lord Drumalbyn sums it up in the Lords, the law sets out the basic responsibilities of employers and employees without adding to the mass of regulations: a general duty of safety “so far as is reasonably practicable,” the same for all employers.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When did the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act receive royal assent, and when did it come into force?
choix: Royal assent on July 31, 1974, in force on October 1, 1974
Royal assent on January 1, 1975, in force immediately the same day
Royal assent in 1972, in force in 1974 after the Robens report
Royal assent on October 1, 1974, in force on July 31, 1975
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The law receives royal assent on July 31, 1974, and comes into force on the following October 1, two months later, according to the law's Wikipedia page.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the formula “so far as is reasonably practicable,” adopted by the 1974 law, come from?
choix: It was invented by the Robens report in 1972 for the occasion
It already appeared in the Coal Mines Act of 1911, and had been interpreted by the courts as early as 1938 and 1949
It comes from a European directive transposed into British law
It was first proposed by Judge Asquith in 1949
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The formula already appeared in the Coal Mines Act of 1911, had been examined in Coltness Iron Co v. Sharp in 1938, and its interpretation was fixed by Edwards v. National Coal Board in 1949; the 1974 law generalizes it without inventing it.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does section 3 of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act of 1974 do?
choix: It limits the duty of safety to the employer's own employees
It bans all mining activity on British territory
It transfers authority over workplace safety to the European Union
It extends a duty of safety toward non-employees, and toward self-employed workers in certain designated activities
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Section 3 extends a duty of safety toward persons who are not the employer's employees, and toward self-employed workers in certain designated activities such as construction, asbestos, or gas.
